content: The global prevalence of leprosy, defined as the number of patients undergoing treatment, was successfully reduced to less than one case per 10,000 population by the year 2000, as per the World Health Assembly (WHA) target. By 2005, this target was achieved at the national level in most endemic countries. However, once this milestone was reached, there was a noticeable complacency among policymakers, support organizations, and healthcare workers. This led to a decline in active case detection efforts, which were deemed less effective and gradually discouraged. Even contact screening was not exempt from this trend. Leprosy services were integrated into general healthcare systems to improve accessibility through primary healthcare, enhance cost-effectiveness, and promote inclusivity. Despite these efforts, the importance of active case detection and contact examination remains critical. The Global Leprosy Update of 2018 highlighted a slow but steady decline in case detection rates, from 244,796 new cases in 2009 to 208,641 in 2018, representing an annual reduction of approximately 2%. However, the persistently high rates of leprosy among children and their proportion of cases indicate ongoing transmission. In 2018, certain regions, including the WHO Americas, Eastern Mediterranean, and Western Pacific, reported an increase in case detection compared to 2017. This rise was attributed to operational factors, such as active case detection campaigns and contact examinations, which uncovered previously hidden cases rather than reflecting a true increase in incidence. The WHO Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020 proposed annual screening of all contacts of leprosy cases for five years as a key intervention, alongside multidrug therapy (MDT) services in low-burden settings. Studies have demonstrated the heightened risk of leprosy among household contacts of patients with multibacillary (MB) leprosy, with a fiveto eight-fold increased risk compared to the general population. Similarly, household contacts of paucibacillary (PB) cases have nearly double the risk of developing leprosy compared to the general community. Research conducted in Bangladesh emphasized the need for early contact examination following the diagnosis of an index case. Additional studies in the Comoros and Bangladesh suggested extending contact examinations beyond households to include neighbors, given the increased risk of leprosy in these groups. Contact tracing is explicitly emphasized under Pillar 2 of the WHO Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020, which focuses on accelerating progress toward a leprosy-free world by promoting active case finding and contact management. Chemoprophylaxis has also been explored as a preventive measure. Early studies using dapsone and acedapsone showed limited success, but more recent research has focused on single-dose rifampicin (SDR). A study conducted in the Marquesas Islands of French Polynesia in 1988 demonstrated a 35–40% reduction in new cases over ten years following SDR chemoprophylaxis. However, subsequent studies in the Pacific Islands and Indonesia yielded mixed results, with some reductions in new cases but inconclusive evidence attributing these declines solely to chemoprophylaxis. A significant breakthrough came with the COLEP trial in Bangladesh (2002–2007), which reported a 57% overall risk reduction in leprosy among contacts receiving SDR. A meta-analysis of 127 studies on chemoprophylaxis found that it provided 60% protection to leprosy contacts. The WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention of Leprosy (2018) recommend chemoprophylaxis as a preventive strategy. The WHO editorial note in 2019 suggested that the gradual reduction in new cases could be further accelerated by introducing SDR chemoprophylaxis, potentially bending the case detection curve toward a leprosy-free world. The feasibility and acceptability of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) using SDR have been assessed in various studies. In Bangladesh, chemoprophylaxis for household contacts was found to be effective and socially acceptable. A feasibility study in Selaru Island, Indonesia, concluded that with adequate planning and investment, a blanket approach to chemoprophylaxis is achievable. In Brazil, the PEP-HANS project highlighted the relevance of PEP in interrupting transmission, preventing new cases, and improving quality of life. The Leprosy Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Programme (LPEP), conducted in multiple countries between 2015 and 2018, demonstrated that contact tracing followed by SDR administration is generally feasible and well-accepted by patients, contacts, and healthcare workers. The cost-effectiveness of SDR-PEP was also confirmed in India, showing benefits in both the short and long term. Despite these advancements, no vaccine or preventive tool has yet been established for routine implementation in leprosy control programs. Based on the available evidence, it is clear that health systems should prioritize contact examination as a critical component of leprosy control. Interventions such as SDR chemoprophylaxis, administered once, are feasible, acceptable, and cost-effective, reducing the risk of leprosy and slowing its transmission. Counseling plays a vital role in leprosy management. Many individuals are unaware that leprosy is curable and that cured patients are no longer infectious. Misconceptions about leprosy being a dreadful disease persist, and many are unaware that prevention is possible even after infection and that disability progression can be managed. Counseling should begin at the time of diagnosis and may require multiple sessions. It can be conducted by professionals or trained peer counselors, including individuals who have experienced leprosy. Patients should be informed about the facts of leprosy, the risk of transmission, treatment options, prevention strategies, and disability management. Consent is crucial in contact tracing. The identity of index cases should only be disclosed with their permission. If an index case refuses to disclose their status, this decision must be respected, and no individual contact screening should occur. In cases where the index case consents to disclose their identity to family members but not to neighbors or social contacts, this preference should also be honored. Community health education should accompany contact tracing efforts, and consent from contacts is required before leprosy screening or offering SDR. In blanket approaches, community leaders' consent must be obtained before initiating PEP campaigns, and individual consent is necessary before administering SDR. If consent is not provided, SDR should not be enforced. The golden hour following a leprosy diagnosis is a critical period for counseling. During this time, patients may experience anxiety about treatment and fear of social stigma. Effective counseling during this period can significantly influence the patient's acceptance of their diagnosis and treatment, as well as their willingness to disclose their condition to family and contacts. Addressing these concerns with sensitivity and providing accurate information can help mitigate the social and emotional impact of leprosy.
